extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians, academic authors, journal editors, and researchers interested in math publishing and computational experiments
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and critique about how mathematics journals (and affiliated editorial systems) should operate, plus recommendations for computational experiments and publishing reproducible work in mathematics.

rubrics_metrics.name: ArXiv-aware submissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Submissions should include arXiv numbers and subject areas because the arXiv is the main dissemination venue in the field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: APS journals encourage including arXiv numbers and subject classifications; unlike Nature/Science, many math/physics journals accept and embrace prior arXiv posting.

rubrics_metrics.name: House style and formatting compliance
rubrics_metrics.description: Submissions must follow the journal's house style (e.g., two-column format, font/length limits) and adhere to word-count rules for letters and articles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PRE requires a two-column house style and has sharp word count limits; authors should take care (including how formulas/tables are counted) because poor formatting can lead to non-expert desk rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Efficient initial screening / desk rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: Editorial offices should perform prompt initial screening (desk rejection) to avoid wasting reviewers' time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PRE desk-rejects about 15-20% of submissions within days; PRL desk rejection is higher (~20-25%); math journals often have even higher desk-rejection rates. Rapid screening saves resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fast review timelines
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals should set and aim for concrete turnaround targets for refereeing and editorial decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At PRE, reviewers are typically given 3 weeks and editors aim to finish the first round in three months so papers can be published within six months; reviewers may get limited extensions (weeks, not months).

rubrics_metrics.name: Active referee recruitment and reasonable expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors should actively recruit multiple referees and be realistic about the number of invitations required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Asking 4–8 potential referees is normal and sometimes 10–20 are needed; difficulty finding referees is a common cause of delay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept/reject/selectivity metrics as signals
rubrics_metrics.description: Acceptance rate and number of papers published are useful descriptive metrics of a journal's selectivity and role.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PRE acceptance ~55–60%, PRL ~20–25%, Nature/Science much lower; numbers contextualize editorial scope but can be misleading due to self-selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rapid production and minimal backlog
rubrics_metrics.description: After acceptance, journals should move quickly through production to online publication and avoid long backlogs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PRE typically sends accepted papers to production and publishes online within 2–3 weeks with effectively zero backlog; prompt production is a feature to emulate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparent appeals process
rubrics_metrics.description: Rejected authors should have a formal, transparent appeals mechanism independent of the original handling editor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PRE sends appeals to members of an Editorial Board who review the paper and referee reports and write a signed report; appeals occur infrequently (~3–5% of rejections). Many math journals lack any appeals process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional editorial staffing and role clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: A mix of full-time professional editors and academic associate editors with clearly defined roles improves handling and continuity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PRE/APS employ full-time PhD editors and university-based associate editors with renewable contracts; roles include Managing Editor, Lead Editor, and (proposed) Chief Editor overseeing operations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial-system transparency for authors
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should be able to see a full log of editorial actions and anonymized referee communications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: APS's system provides a complete log of dates and anonymized referee actions; this level of transparency is superior to typical math journal systems that only show 'under review'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Team-based editorial queue management
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors should operate as a team with shared queues so that individual editor inactivity does not stall papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At PRE, routines (forwarding revisions, managing emails) are handled by the first available person while substantive decisions remain with the assigned Associate Editor; queues are redistributed if someone is inactive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-journal coordination and transfer
rubrics_metrics.description: Editorial systems should allow editors across related journals to see reports and transfer/cascade suitable submissions to appropriate sister journals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: APS systems allow editors to view reports across journals (e.g., PRL → PRE) to invite appropriate rejections; transfer features in some publisher systems exist but are often blocked by firewalls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasis on readability and style
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals should value readable, well-styled papers; poor style can cause rejection by non-expert editors/referees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PRE emphasizes shorter, more readable papers and good style; authors should polish exposition to avoid avoidable desk rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support for survey/expository work
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals should solicit and publish surveys and expository articles because they serve community needs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: APS publishes Reviews of Modern Physics and occasionally solicits 'perspectives'; mathematics has comparatively few venues for high-profile surveys, making such solicitation valuable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial highlighting (Editors' Suggestions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals can formally highlight a small number of notable papers to increase visibility and provide recognition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PRE introduced 'Editors' Suggestions' to spotlight selected articles; such badges can be listed on CVs and aid author recognition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Referee recognition programs
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals should recognize outstanding referees formally to incentivize high-quality, timely reviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: APS's Distinguished Referee Award (since 2008) honors hundreds of referees across journals annually and is taken seriously; smaller awards could be adopted by math journals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community-oriented editorial mission
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals should view themselves as community service: validate significance, help authors improve presentation, and be welcoming to newcomers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PRE is described as functioning like a 'digital local newspaper'—fast, supportive, and community-minded, in contrast to adversarial or purely commercial models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding profit-driven degradation of standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals must resist profit incentives that could lower editorial standards or create low-quality 'mass publication' outlets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: APS journals generate revenue but maintain editorial standards; the post warns of attempts to create lower-tier venues to monetize more rejections, implying vigilance is needed to preserve quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: ArXiv and preprint policy clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals should have clear policies about arXiv/preprint postings and not penalize authors for prior dissemination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: APS journals encourage arXiv usage, whereas some high-profile journals (Nature/Science) forbid prior posting; authors should be aware of and comply with journal policies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Solicitation and modest payment/incentives for commissioned pieces
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals can proactively commission perspectives or surveys and offer modest payments to incentivize timely completion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviews of Modern Physics offers modest payments ($1,500 or $750) for survey-like pieces to ensure timely delivery; targeted solicitation helps secure high-quality expository content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publish reproducible computational work and share code
rubrics_metrics.description: When using computers/Monte Carlo experiments, authors should design careful experiments, share code and notes publicly (e.g., GitHub), and post results (including negative/failed experiments) to arXiv.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author urges making code and work notes publicly available and recommends placing work on arXiv if journals decline; universities or companies may supply compute resources on request.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of Monte Carlo evidence in mathematics
rubrics_metrics.description: Purely statistical/Monte Carlo evidence (e.g., 99.99% confidence) is insufficient for formal mathematical claims; journals generally prefer 100% correctness (formal proofs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monte Carlo testing can't formally disprove a conjecture (since it samples subgraphs); math journals usually require formal arguments and would likely refuse to accept a 'five-sigma' counterexample without a rigorous proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publish negative results and failed computational investigations
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should not fear publishing failed computational efforts because such reports prevent duplication and are useful to the community.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author recommends publishing negative or failed computational experiments (on arXiv if necessary) so others avoid repeating the same mistakes; this is part of responsible scholarship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain editorial appeal/check mechanisms for subjectivity of importance
rubrics_metrics.description: Because 'importance' is subjective, journals should build appeals and checks (e.g., editorial board reviews) to moderate Associate Editor decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: APS uses an Editorial Board (a board of appeals) whose members review appeals and sign reports; such institutional checks help moderate subjective judgments about significance.
